answer.sourceLine: King preached this thought in near-identical words in “When Peace Becomes Obnoxious,” a sermon delivered 18 March 1956 at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery and published in the Louisville Defender on 29 March 1956: “But peace is not merely the absence of this tension, but the presence of justice.” The compressed one-line form that circulates today is recorded in King’s own 1964 collection A Martin Luther King Treasury.

source.excerpt: I agree that it is more tension now. But peace is not merely the absence of this tension, but the presence of justice.
trail: Circa 1954–1955 — the wording people quote. Quote Investigator traces the exact one-liner to King’s own account of a conversation, printed in A Martin Luther King Treasury (Educational Heritage, Yonkers, 1964), chapter 2, page 30 — verified on paper ↗.

18 March 1956 — the same argument, from the pulpit. A year or two later, preaching the morning before his bus-boycott trial, King made the point again in near-identical words, recounting a recent conversation about the bus protest: “But peace is not merely the absence of this tension, but the presence of justice.” The sermon was published in the Louisville Defender on 29 March 1956 and is reprinted in the King Papers ↗. It is an independent primary attestation of the idea, not the occasion Quote Investigator gives for the compressed sentence.

26 April 1957 — he kept using it. Quote Investigator cites a speech report in the Montgomery Alabama Tribune, page 6: “I come not to bring this old peace which is merely the absence of tension; I come to bring a positive peace which is the presence of justice” ↗.

Cross-check. Wikiquote lists the one-line form in its sourced 1950s section, citing Stephen B. Oates’s biography Let the Trumpet Sound (1982) and tying it to the Montgomery bus boycott — see the entry ↗.
source.excerptNote: King is recounting a conversation about the bus boycott with a man who complained that the protest had destroyed the peace of the community. The sentence that circulates today — “True peace is not merely the absence of tension; it is the presence of justice” — is the same argument in tightened form; Quote Investigator dates the compressed sentence to a separate conversation circa 1954–1955, verifying that exact wording on page 30 of King’s 1964 collection.

The sermon was first published in the Louisville Defender on 29 March 1956 and the compressed wording in A Martin Luther King Treasury in 1964 — both within the US copyright term for renewed works, and King’s estate actively registers and enforces rights in his words, so no public-domain claim is available here. The scholarly edition quoted here appears in The Papers of Martin Luther King, Jr., vol. 3, published by the University of California Press. Short quotation with attribution is ordinary fair use; reproducing the sermon is not.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.heading: About Martin Luther King Jr.
author.metaLine: 1929–1968 · Baptist minister and leader of the American civil rights movement
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. was pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, Alabama, when the bus boycott began in December 1955 — he was, as the King Institute puts it, a twenty-six-year-old minister, serving in only his second year as pastor. The contrast between a negative peace (mere quiet) and a positive peace (justice actually present) became one of his signature arguments, and he returned to it for years. It is the spine of his most quoted paragraph in the Letter from Birmingham Jail of 16 April 1963, where he names the white moderate “who prefers a negative peace which is the absence of tension to a positive peace which is the presence of justice.”

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: This one is real — the errors are about where King said it, and about a look-alike sentence that travels under a different name.

items.why: The Letter of 16 April 1963 is constantly cited for this one-liner, but it does not contain it. What it contains is the fuller argument the line compresses: King names the white moderate “who prefers a negative peace which is the absence of tension to a positive peace which is the presence of justice” ↗. Same idea, different sentence, and seven years after the Montgomery sermon that stated it plainly.

A near-twin sentence — “True peace is not merely the absence of war, it is the presence of justice” — circulates widely under Jane Addams’s name. On the user-submitted page where it spreads ↗ no book, essay or speech is named, and the site notes such quotes are not verified. We found no primary Addams source for it. The Jane Addams Hull-House Museum used “True Peace: The Presence of Justice” as an exhibition title, which is not the same as attributing the sentence to her.

items.who: Dorothy Thompson and other pre-war writers
items.why: The shape of the sentence predates King. Quote Investigator documents a 17 September 1938 letter in the Bergen Evening Record — “But peace is more than absence of armed conflict” — and columnist Dorothy Thompson in 1945: “Peace is not the mere absence of war. It is a positive condition of justice.” ↗ These are thematic ancestors, not the source of King’s wording.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s verdict is unambiguous: “Martin Luther King Jr. deserves credit for the statement” ↗, recorded in his 1964 collection and spoken in Montgomery years earlier.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: King preached “When Peace Becomes Obnoxious” from his own pulpit on the morning before he faced trial for his part in the Montgomery bus boycott. His target was a newspaper headline out of Tuscaloosa — “Things are quiet in Tuscaloosa today” — printed after a mob drove Autherine Lucy, the first Black student admitted to the University of Alabama, off campus. Quiet had been restored. King’s point was that quiet is not the same thing as peace.

The line lands the way it does because it is an argument, not a sentiment. It reframes the accusation constantly aimed at the boycott — that it was creating trouble — by conceding the tension and denying that its absence was ever worth anything. King spent the next decade sharpening the same distinction, and it reaches its most famous form in the Letter from Birmingham Jail.
detailsBody: Having drawn the distinction, King made it concrete with a list of the things a merely quiet peace would cost, each opening the same way: if peace means accepting second-class citizenship, keeping silent in the midst of injustice, being complacently adjusted to a deadening status quo, or submitting to exploitation and domination — then he does not want it. The passage closes: “So in a passive, non-violent manner, we must revolt against this peace.”

The sermon survives only because Louisville Defender editor Frank L. Stanley was in Montgomery covering King’s trial, transcribed it, and sent the text to King for review before running it on 29 March 1956. Much of King’s early preaching was never recorded at all.
context.pull: Quiet had been restored. King’s point was that quiet is not the same thing as peace.
